news.title: ‘This is the dream job’: Labour’s Bev Craig on the battle to be Greater Manchester mayor
news.summary:
Polling puts close Burnham ally in lead as she aims to defeat Reform and draw back support from revitalised Greens

Bev Craig was mid-squat at the gym when she was recognised for the first time as the prospective heir to Andy Burnham’s throne. Until recently, the Manchester city council leader could happily have gone about her workout in peace.

But all that changed when Burnham, who DJ’ed at her 40th birthday party last year, won the Makerfield byelection and set up another big electoral contest on his way to becoming prime minister.

news_drafts.headline: Manchester's £500m capital plan depends on £71.5m in uncertain property sales as inflation data vanishes
news_drafts.lead: Manchester's four-year capital programme relies on generating £71.5m from land and building disposals to avoid either cutting planned projects or borrowing more, according to capital monitoring papers reviewed by the Executive this week. The council holds £98.1m in capital receipts reserves but needs £104.8m immediately to fund its approved programme. Officers warned that if the timing of disposals falters, the council would need to reduce the programme or borrow additional funds. The risk deepens because the council cannot forecast specific inflation impact on construction costs: the Office for National Statistics has suspended publication of construction material price indices due to a methodology error. With consumer price inflation at 2.9% and rising, the council's £30m contingency budget for the capital programme may prove inadequate without visibility of actual construction cost trends.

news_drafts.headline: Manchester faces £7.7m Adult Social Care overspend as planned savings prove undeliverable
news_drafts.lead: Manchester City Council is forecasting a £7.7m overspend in adult social care by the end of the financial year, with the shortfall driven partly by the failure of a planned transformation programme to deliver savings. The council budgeted to save £2.5m from a "Care Closer to Home" efficiency scheme, but the papers show the planned savings are undelivered because their benefits have "inconclusive" modelling. The overspend has widened by £326,000 since July. Pressures include a rise in demand: 25 more supported accommodation clients than budgeted, 36 additional complex learning disability cases, and 44 extra mental health care packages. Officers warn that any further demand growth will increase the overspend unless new cost reductions or efficiencies are found in-year.

news_drafts.headline: Manchester Town Hall refurbishment overruns by £27m as capital programme strains finances
news_drafts.lead: Manchester's flagship Town Hall refurbishment has exceeded its annual budget by £27.1m, now forecast to cost £113.6m against an approved £86.5m allocation, the council's Executive heard on 16 September. Completion has been delayed to 2027. The overrun represents the largest single variance in the council's capital programme and comes as the authority faces broader financing pressures: its current reserves of £98.1m fall short of the £104.8m immediately needed to fund approved projects, forcing reliance on generating a further £71.5m from land and building sales over the next four years. The council also faces new structural liabilities, including £7.5m in repairs to the Arndale Car Park required under lease obligations and £7.1m in new borrowing to replace homelessness accommodation lost when Woodward Court became unfit for purpose.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – Proposed changes to the capital programme.
findings.headline: Off-street parking expansion of £7.5m (2027/28–2028/29) financed through borrowing on 'invest to save' basis
findings.detail: Manchester is allocating £3.75m in 2027/28 and £3.75m in 2028/29 to off-street parking improvements funded through borrowing on an invest-to-save basis, assuming parking revenues will service the debt.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether parking revenue projections are realistic and whether existing parking investments have delivered the returns on which this multi-year expansion depends.
findings.quote: Off Street Parking - Further Works Borrowing on an invest to save basis 3,750 3,750 7,500

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – Proposed changes to the capital programme.
findings.headline: Manchester funding £4.85m in homelessness accommodation through capital borrowing on 'invest to save' basis
findings.detail: Two homelessness accommodation schemes—Slade Lane (£2.75m) and The Works (£2.1m)—are being capital-funded through borrowing on an invest-to-save basis. This financing approach for homelessness services is unusual and assumes these facilities will generate sufficient income to service the debt.
findings.matters: Homelessness services typically cannot generate revenue income; this financing model requires realistic assumptions about income generation and warrants scrutiny from a lender's perspective.
findings.quote: Homelessness Accommodation - Slade Lane Borrowing on an invest to save basis 2,750; Homelessness Accommodation - The Works Borrowing on an invest to save basis 2,100

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 – Proposed changes to the capital programme.
findings.headline: Manchester committing £14.6m to new capital schemes financed through borrowing on 'invest to save' basis
findings.detail: The council is requesting approval for £14.6m in capital spending financed through borrowing on an invest-to-save basis. Schemes include Mauldeth House Development (£2.25m), homelessness accommodation at Slade Lane (£2.75m) and The Works (£2.1m), and off-street parking expansion (£7.5m). All are expected to generate sufficient income to service the borrowing.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council is overreliant on income-generating capital schemes, and whether existing invest-to-save projects are delivering expected returns to justify further borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Report to the end of July 2026
findings.headline: General Fund projected £7.4m overspend, up £1.4m month-on-month, requiring call on reserves with no recovery plan in view
findings.detail: The council's overall revenue position is deteriorating, with projected overspend increasing by £1.4m since the previous month. The deterioration spans Adult Social Care, Neighbourhoods, and Growth & Development. The council will call on General Fund reserves to balance the year, with no quantified mitigation plan to recover the position.
findings.matters: Month-on-month deterioration signals declining budget control; reserve depletion reduces financial flexibility to respond to future pressures or shocks
findings.figures: £7.4m General Fund overspend; £1.4m increase from previous month's forecast
findings.quote: The current forecast is an overspend of £7.4m, an increase of £1.4m since last reported to the Executive

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Report to the end of July 2026
findings.headline: DSG deficit accumulated to £59.2m; statutory override expires March 2028 with government write-off proposed but unconfirmed, leaving contingent liability
findings.detail: Manchester's cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £59.2m by March 2026. The government has proposed writing off 90% (£53.3m) but this is not yet confirmed, leaving a residual £5.9m that would fall to the General Fund. The statutory override that currently excludes this deficit from council reserves expires March 2028, placing the council at potential Section 114 notice risk.
findings.matters: A contingent General Fund liability of £5.9m to £14m poses long-term balance sheet risk; section 114 jeopardy reflects loss of financial control if deficits continue
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit to March 2026: £59.2m; government write-off proposed: 90% (£53.3m); residual: £5.9m; 2026/27 forecast deficit: £34.0m; 2027/28 forecast: £80.7m; EHCPs increased 10.3% year-on-year (9,402 to 10,359 June 2025–2026); statutory override expires March 2028
findings.quote: However, this override is to expire in March 2028 and for many authorities without intervention this would place them at risk of issuing a Section 114 notice.
